text: Dates and times look simple until you look closely. This lesson covers date and time types across platforms, including one Oracle quirk that catches almost everyone who moves from SQL Server.
Your baseline: date, time, datetime two for modern higher-precision timestamps, and datetime offset when you need an explicit timezone. Four distinct types, each with a clear job.

Oracle's quirk: its DATE type is never truly date-only. It always stores a time component, down to the second, even when you're only thinking about the date. Compare two Oracle dates expecting them to be equal, and hidden time values can quietly break that assumption.

MySQL has a real, documented gotcha of its own: datetime and timestamp. Datetime has a wider range and is not timezone-aware. Timestamp is timezone-aware, stored in U-T-C and converted on retrieval, but has a narrower supported range. Choose based on which behavior you actually need.
PostgreSQL keeps it a bit simpler: timestamp with no timezone awareness, and timestamptz, which handles timezone information explicitly -- playing a similar role to SQL Server's datetime offset.
Next lesson: boolean, a type that doesn't really exist natively on most of these platforms. See you there.
